before.q: Trade can make people better off because:
options: People can specialize and exchange
Everyone becomes self-sufficient
Scarcity disappears
Prices no longer matter
before.feedback: Trade allows specialization and exchange, which can benefit both sides.

after.q: Two neighbors specialize in the chores for which each gives up less valuable alternative work, then exchange help. Why can both benefit?
options: Specialization can raise combined output available to share
Exchange makes both neighbors completely self-sufficient under an incorrect opportunity-cost interpretation
Scarcity disappears once the chores are divided
The faster neighbor must perform every chore
after.commonError: Treating trade as zero-sum or assigning every task to the fastest producer.
after.feedback: Different opportunity costs can make specialization and voluntary exchange beneficial.

before.q: Comparative advantage is determined by comparing:
options: Opportunity costs between producers.
Total output without considering tradeoffs.
Hourly wages in unrelated jobs.
The money price charged after trade.
before.commonError: Using absolute output instead of opportunity cost.
before.feedback: Comparative advantage belongs to the producer with the lower opportunity cost.

after.q: Mira gives up 1 report to prepare a presentation; Sol gives up 3 reports. Which fact determines comparative advantage in presentations?
options: Mira gives up fewer reports per presentation
Sol may complete more total tasks in a day
Mira charges a lower money price after exchange
Sol has a higher wage in an unrelated job
after.commonError: Using total output, wages, or prices instead of opportunity cost.
after.feedback: Comparative advantage belongs to the lower-opportunity-cost producer.

before.q: A producer has an absolute advantage in a good when the producer can:
options: Give up less of every other good.
Make more of the good with the same resources.
Set the market price without competition.
Eliminate scarcity by specializing.
before.commonError: Treating absolute and comparative advantage as the same idea.
before.feedback: Absolute advantage concerns productivity; comparative advantage concerns opportunity cost.

after.q: With the same resources, East Farm can harvest 12 crates while West Farm can harvest 8. What does this establish?
options: East Farm has an absolute advantage in harvesting crates
East Farm must have comparative advantage in every crop under an incorrect opportunity-cost interpretation
West Farm has the lower opportunity cost of harvesting
Both farms gain equally from every possible exchange
after.commonError: Inferring comparative advantage from productivity alone.
after.feedback: Greater output from the same resources establishes absolute, not necessarily comparative, advantage.

before.q: A tariff raises the domestic cost of an imported good. Which effect most directly reduces gains from trade?
options: It eliminates all domestic production.
It makes opportunity cost irrelevant.
It guarantees that consumers gain more than producers lose.
It discourages exchanges that reflected differences in opportunity cost.
before.commonError: Treating a trade barrier as costless redistribution.
before.feedback: A tariff can block mutually beneficial trades and reduce the gains available from specialization.

after.q: A region can obtain one turbine by giving up 3 tons of grain through exchange or 5 tons by producing it internally. Which reasoning supports exchange?
options: Importing the turbine has the lower opportunity cost in grain
Producing internally must be better because it avoids trade under an incorrect opportunity-cost interpretation
The money price eliminates the need to compare resources
Exchange guarantees equal gains for every resident
after.commonError: Preferring self-sufficiency without comparing opportunity costs.
after.feedback: Exchange uses resources worth 3 tons rather than 5, freeing 2 tons for other uses.

before.q: A country exports a good in which it has comparative advantage. Domestic consumers of that good face a higher price after trade opens. Which statement is most complete?
options: The country can gain overall even though some domestic groups lose.
Every resident must gain because national output rises.
Trade cannot create gains when any group loses.
The higher price proves the country lacks comparative advantage.
before.commonError: Confusing aggregate gains with universal gains.
before.feedback: Trade can raise total surplus while distributing gains and losses unevenly.

after.q: Two firms specialize and create 40 extra units of combined output. A proposed exchange gives all 40 extra units to one firm. What is the strongest conclusion?
options: Specialization created aggregate gains, but the proposed distribution may not benefit both firms
Comparative advantage is false whenever gains are unequal under an incorrect opportunity-cost interpretation
Any increase in combined output makes every exchange mutually beneficial
Equal gains are required before specialization can raise output
after.commonError: Confusing total gains with mutual benefit under a particular exchange.
after.feedback: Higher combined output creates potential gains; terms of trade determine how those gains are divided.

before.q: A trade price equals the exporter’s opportunity cost exactly but is below the importer’s opportunity cost. Which side captures the modeled gain?
options: The exporter captures all gain.
Both capture equal gains.
Neither can gain because the price is below both costs.
The importer captures the gain; the exporter is indifferent at that price.
before.commonError: Assuming every price inside or on the bounds divides gains equally.
before.feedback: At its own opportunity cost, the exporter is indifferent; the importer still saves resources.

after.q: A trade rate equals the exporter’s opportunity cost exactly but remains below the importer’s opportunity cost. Which evaluation is precise?

after.feedback: At its own opportunity cost the exporter is indifferent; the importer still saves resources.

after.q: Ava’s cost of one crate is 2 sacks; Ben’s is 5 sacks. At exactly 2 sacks per crate, which statement is correct?

Both receive strict gains from the trade under an incorrect opportunity-cost interpretation
Ben is indifferent and Ava captures every gain
The rate lies strictly between their opportunity costs
after.commonError: Including a boundary or a rate outside the two opportunity costs as a strict mutual gain.
after.feedback: A strict mutual-gain rate lies strictly between the relevant opportunity costs.

after.q: One bolt costs East 0.5 panel and West 1.25 panels. Which interval states strict mutual-gain rates in panels per bolt?
options: More than 0.5 but less than 1.25 panels per bolt
More than 2 but less than 4 bolts per panel under an incorrect opportunity-cost interpretation
At least 0.5 and at most 1.25 panels per bolt
Less than 0.5 panels per bolt only
after.commonError: Including a boundary or a rate outside the two opportunity costs as a strict mutual gain.
after.feedback: A strict mutual-gain rate lies strictly between the relevant opportunity costs.

after.q: A consultant completes more audits and presentations than an associate. A manager concludes the consultant should do both. What is missing?
options: The opportunity cost of assigning the consultant to each task
The consultant’s absolute output in both tasks under an incorrect opportunity-cost interpretation
A guarantee that specialization divides gains equally
The money price of international exports
after.commonError: Using greater output alone to assign comparative advantage.
after.feedback: Absolute advantage concerns productivity; comparative advantage concerns lower opportunity cost.

after.q: Specialization raises combined output, but a proposed exchange rate lies above both producers’ costs for the exported good. What follows?
options: Higher output creates potential gains, but this rate will not benefit both sides
Every feasible exchange shares the production gain under an incorrect opportunity-cost interpretation
The higher-cost producer now has comparative advantage
Both sides are strictly better off because specialization occurred
after.commonError: Assuming higher combined output makes every possible exchange mutually beneficial.
after.feedback: Specialization creates potential output gains; the trading terms determine whether both sides gain.

before.q: A project lead is faster at every task but delegates data entry. Which concept explains the choice?
options: A binding price ceiling.
Absolute advantage in data entry.
Comparative advantage based on the opportunity cost of the lead’s time.
The elimination of scarcity.
before.commonError: Failing to transfer comparative advantage to workplace allocation.
before.feedback: Comparative advantage applies whenever limited time can be allocated among tasks.

after.q: A project lead is faster at every task but delegates data entry. Which concept explains the choice?
options: A price ceiling that limits payment for outsourced data entry
Absolute advantage because the lead is faster at data entry
Comparative advantage based on the opportunity cost of the lead's time
Elimination of scarce time after the work is delegated
after.commonError: Using absolute productivity instead of the opportunity cost of the lead's time.
after.feedback: Delegation can be efficient when the lead has a higher opportunity cost of doing data entry.

before.q: A city can buy snowplow service from a neighboring county for less than the resources required to provide it internally. The opportunity-cost logic suggests:
options: The city must produce every service itself.
The neighboring county cannot gain.
Money prices eliminate opportunity costs.
Contracting can free city resources for other services.
before.commonError: Failing to apply gains-from-trade logic to public-service contracting.
before.feedback: Buying a service can release resources when the external cost is below the internal opportunity cost.

after.q: A city can buy snowplow service from a neighboring county for less than the resources required to provide it internally. What does opportunity-cost reasoning suggest?
options: The city should remain self-sufficient even at a higher resource cost
The neighboring county cannot benefit from any voluntary contract
Money prices make the city's forgone alternatives irrelevant
Contracting can free city resources for other services
after.commonError: Ignoring the internal resources forgone when the city provides the service itself.
after.feedback: Buying the service at lower opportunity cost frees scarce city resources for other uses.
